claims.text: In2O3 is a selective and durable catalyst for gas-phase CO2 hydrogenation to methanol.
Pd atoms can replace indium atoms in the active In3O5 ensemble.
Substitutional Pd enhances H2 activation in Pd-promoted In2O3.
Improved H2 activation favors methanol formation.
Atomically dispersed Pd prevents formation of the multi-atom Pd sites required for RWGS.
Controlled co-precipitation can produce the proposed substitutional Pd architecture and associated low-nuclearity Pd clusters.
Conventional deposition produces Pd nanoparticles on In2O3.
The proposed comparison applies under industrially relevant gas-phase CO2-hydrogenation temperatures and pressures.
Substitutional Pd attracts additional surface Pd atoms, forming low-nuclearity clusters near active sites.
Low-nuclearity Pd species provide activated hydrogen for methanol synthesis.
Larger Pd nanoparticles mediate parasitic RWGS and thereby reduce methanol selectivity.
Atomically dispersed or low-nuclearity Pd will deliver higher methanol productivity than nanoparticle Pd on In2O3.
Atomically dispersed or low-nuclearity Pd will provide higher methanol selectivity and lower RWGS activity than nanoparticle Pd.
The atomically dispersed or low-nuclearity Pd catalyst will maintain performance for 500 hours.
Pd nanoparticles on In2O3 can sinter or alloy with indium, limiting metal utilization and robustness.
The hypothesis is restricted to Pd loadings that prevent alloy formation with indium.
The hypothesis holds only where H2 activation is kinetically controlling.
The exact atomic-scale interaction between substituted Pd and the oxide matrix is unresolved and may not be the only structural factor controlling performance.
Atomic-resolution characterization can distinguish the substitutional or atomically dispersed state from Pd nanoparticles in the proposed comparison.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in productivity, selectivity, and durability relative to the nanoparticle control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says atomically dispersed Pd prevents the multi-atom sites required for RWGS, while the intervention and mediator explicitly propose formation of low-nuclearity Pd clusters, which are themselves multi-atom species. The distinction between benign low-nuclearity clusters and RWGS-active larger ensembles is not defined.
